title: The Delhi Sultanate
description: An illustrated map of the Delhi Sultanate, from the Ghurid victory at Tarain in 1192, through the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi sultans, to Babur’s victory at Panipat in 1526.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Delhi Sultanate from 1000 to 1526
note: Based on the Persian chronicles of the time (Minhaj-i Siraj, Amir Khusrau, Barani, Afif), Ibn Battuta’s travels, Rajput and Sufi traditions and modern historians; each chapter says which it follows. Army sizes, treasure and death tolls from chronicles are given as they state them and are disputed. The map is stylised and not to scale, and the Powers areas are painted loosely: borders shifted constantly.

court.name: The court and the people of Delhi

steps.title: Raiders from the hills
steps.text: From Ghazni, Sultan Mahmud raids north India about seventeen times between 1000 and 1027, sacking Mathura and Somnath, but rules only the Punjab. A century later the Ghurids, from the mountains of Ghor, take Ghazni. In 1173 Muhammad of Ghor becomes its ruler, and in 1186 he takes Lahore from the last Ghaznavid king.
steps.today: Today: Ghazni, Afghanistan.

steps.title: The battles of Tarain
steps.text: In 1191 Prithviraj Chauhan, king of Ajmer and Delhi, defeats Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain, and Muhammad is carried wounded from the field. He returns in 1192 with a larger army of mounted archers and wins. Persian sources say Prithviraj was captured and put to death; a later poem, the Prithviraj Raso, tells a different, legendary ending.
steps.today: Today: Taraori, near Karnal, Haryana.

steps.title: The saint of Ajmer
steps.text: Muinuddin Chishti, a Sufi teacher born in Sistan, settles in Ajmer, the Chauhan capital, about the time of the conquest; tradition sets his arrival just before or after Tarain. He teaches love of God and service to the poor, and welcomes all comers. He dies in 1236, and his tomb (dargah) becomes one of South Asia’s great shrines.
steps.today: Today: the Dargah Sharif, Ajmer, Rajasthan, visited by people of every faith.

steps.title: A tower of victory
steps.text: Muhammad leaves his Indian conquests to Qutbuddin Aibak, a Turkish slave he had bought and raised to command. Aibak takes Delhi and builds a mosque whose inscription says it used material from 27 temples. About 1199 he begins the Qutb Minar; his successor Iltutmish adds three storeys. Whether it is named for Aibak or a saint is debated.
steps.today: Today: the Qutb Minar and its monuments, Mehrauli, Delhi, a World Heritage site.

steps.title: Bakhtiyar in the east
steps.text: Bakhtiyar Khalji, a Ghurid commander, raids Bihar and storms a walled monastery that the historian Minhaj says was full of shaven-headed scholars and books; it is usually identified as Odantapuri. Whether he also destroyed Nalanda is debated. He surprises the Sena king at Nadia and rules from Lakhnauti, but dies in 1206 after a disastrous march toward Tibet.
steps.today: Today: Bihar Sharif, Bihar, stands on Odantapuri’s site.

steps.title: A slave becomes sultan
steps.text: In 1206 Muhammad of Ghor is killed on his way back to Ghazni. Aibak takes power at Lahore, the first of the Delhi sultans; because he and several successors began as slaves (mamluks), they are called the Mamluk or Slave dynasty. Remembered as ‘giver of lakhs’ (lakh bakhsh) for his generosity, he dies in 1210 after a fall at polo.
steps.today: Today: Aibak’s tomb stands in Anarkali Bazaar, Lahore, Pakistan.

steps.title: Chinggis Khan on the Indus
steps.text: Chinggis Khan’s Mongols chase Jalaluddin, prince of Khwarazm, to the Indus and defeat him there in 1221; its exact site is uncertain. Jalaluddin swims the river and asks Delhi for refuge. Sultan Iltutmish, unwilling to draw the Mongols in, declines. Chinggis turns back, but Mongol raids will trouble the sultanate for nearly a century.
steps.today: Today: the Indus near Attock, Pakistan, is the usual guess for the site.

steps.title: Iltutmish
steps.text: Iltutmish, another former slave and Aibak’s son-in-law, makes Delhi the capital and defeats his rivals in Sindh and Bengal. In 1229 envoys of the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad confirm him as sultan. He issues a silver coin (tanka) and copper jital, and rules with a circle of Turkish nobles later called ‘the Forty’.
steps.today: Today: his tomb, Delhi’s oldest surviving royal tomb, stands in the Qutb complex.

steps.title: Razia, sultan
steps.text: Iltutmish names his daughter Razia as heir. The historian Minhaj says she put aside women’s dress, wore a coat and cap, and rode out on an elephant before her people. Nobles resent her and her favourite, Yaqut, an Abyssinian. Altunia, governor of Bathinda, rebels; she marries him, but both are killed near Kaithal in 1240.
steps.today: Today: Bathinda, Punjab, where Razia was held in the fort.

steps.title: Balban and the frontier
steps.text: Balban, the power behind the throne for twenty years, becomes sultan in 1266. He insists on prostration at court and calls the king God’s shadow on earth. He guards the northwest against the Mongols, but in 1285 his favourite son, Prince Muhammad, is killed fighting them near Multan. The young poet Amir Khusrau, in the prince’s service, is captured.
steps.today: Today: Multan, Punjab, Pakistan.

steps.title: Gold from Devagiri
steps.text: In 1290 the Khaljis, Turks long settled in Afghanistan, take the throne. In 1296 Alauddin, the sultan’s nephew and governor of Kara, crosses the Vindhyas without leave and raids Devagiri, capital of the Yadavas. He returns with a huge ransom, has his uncle killed when he comes to greet him at Kara, and takes the throne.
steps.today: Today: Daulatabad fort, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad), Maharashtra.

steps.title: A slave from Khambhat
steps.text: Alauddin’s generals invade Gujarat in 1299. The Vaghela king Karna flees, and the Somnath temple is sacked again. At the rich port of Khambhat the general Nusrat Khan seizes a eunuch slave named Kafur, said to have been bought for a thousand dinars. Given to Alauddin, Malik Kafur rises to command his armies.
steps.today: Today: Khambhat, Gujarat, on the Gulf of Khambhat.

steps.title: Mongols at the gates
steps.text: The Mongols of Central Asia invade again and again. In 1299 a huge army reaches Kili, just outside Delhi, and Alauddin’s general Zafar Khan dies holding it back. In 1303 the Mongols besiege Delhi for about two months while the army is away. Alauddin entrenches at Siri, later walls it as a new city, and wins in 1305 and 1306.
steps.today: Today: traces of Siri’s walls survive near Shahpur Jat, south Delhi.

steps.title: Ranthambore and Chittor
steps.text: Alauddin takes the Rajput forts of Ranthambore, from Hammira Chauhan in 1301, and Chittor, from Ratnasimha in 1303, after long sieges. Amir Khusrau, who came on the Chittor campaign, gives a large death toll that is disputed. The famous story of Queen Padmini first appears in Malik Muhammad Jayasi’s poem Padmavat, written in 1540.
steps.today: Today: Chittorgarh and Ranthambore forts, Rajasthan, World Heritage sites.

steps.title: Markets and prices
steps.text: To pay a large standing army against the Mongols, Alauddin sets fixed prices in Delhi’s markets for grain, cloth, horses and slaves, and stores grain against famine. In the land between the Ganges and Yamuna he takes half the harvest as tax. Soldiers’ horses are branded to stop fraud. The historian Barani, writing later, describes it all.
steps.today: Today: the Alai Darwaza (1311), Alauddin’s gateway, stands in the Qutb complex.

steps.title: Warangal pays tribute
steps.text: Malik Kafur marches south through Devagiri and besieges Warangal, the Kakatiya capital. In 1310 King Prataparudra submits, handing over treasure, elephants and horses and promising yearly tribute. Alauddin wants wealth and loyalty from the south, not direct rule. Amir Khusrau tells the campaign in his history of Alauddin’s victories (Khazain al-Futuh).
steps.today: Today: Warangal fort and its carved stone gateways, Telangana.

steps.title: To the far south
steps.text: In 1311 Kafur reaches Dwarasamudra, where the Hoysala king Ballala III submits, then marches into the Pandya country, where two royal brothers are at war. He sacks temples and raids Madurai, though neither brother is caught. He returns to Delhi with vast treasure, by the chroniclers’ count hundreds of elephants and thousands of horses.
steps.today: Today: Madurai, Tamil Nadu; Halebidu, Karnataka, was Dwarasamudra.

steps.title: Delhi is still far
steps.text: After Alauddin dies in 1316 the Khaljis fall in murders and plots. In 1320 Ghazi Malik, a frontier general, takes the throne as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq and builds the fortress city of Tughlaqabad. Tradition says that, angry with the Sufi Nizamuddin Auliya, he heard: ‘Delhi is still far.’ Returning from Bengal in 1325, he dies when a pavilion collapses.
steps.today: Today: the ruined walls of Tughlaqabad, south Delhi.

steps.title: A capital moved south
steps.text: Ghiyasuddin’s son, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, is learned and restless. In 1327 he makes Devagiri, renamed Daulatabad, a second capital to rule the south, and orders much of Delhi’s elite to move there, over a thousand kilometres. Barani describes the suffering of the journey. Within a few years many are allowed to return.
steps.today: Today: Daulatabad fort, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Brass for silver
steps.text: Short of silver, Muhammad issues brass and copper coins to pass at the value of silver ones. People forge them in huge numbers, and trade falters. After a few years he withdraws the tokens and exchanges them for real coin from the treasury. Barani says heaps of them lay at Tughlaqabad. A planned conquest of Khurasan is also abandoned.
steps.today: Today: the token coins survive in museum collections.

steps.title: Ibn Battuta
steps.text: Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan traveller, reaches Delhi in 1334 and is made a judge (qazi). He calls the sultan the man most given to making gifts and to shedding blood. In 1342 he is sent as envoy to China, but his ships are wrecked at Calicut. He goes on alone and later dictates his travels (the Rihla) in Morocco.
steps.today: Today: Kozhikode (Calicut), Kerala.

steps.title: An empire breaks apart
steps.text: Famine, heavy taxes and harsh punishments spark revolts. Madurai breaks away in 1335, Vijayanagara is founded about 1336, Bengal goes its own way, and in 1347 Deccan nobles crown Hasan Bahman Shah at Gulbarga, founding the Bahmani sultanate. Muhammad dies in 1351 chasing a rebel near Thatta. Badauni later writes that king and people were freed of each other.
steps.today: Today: Kalaburagi (Gulbarga), Karnataka, with its Bahmani fort and mosque.

steps.title: Ashoka’s pillars move to Delhi
steps.text: Muhammad’s cousin Firuz Shah rules gently with his nobles, though harshly toward Hindus, extending the jizya tax to Brahmins. He digs canals, founds towns such as Hisar and Jaunpur, and builds Firozabad beside Delhi. He has two of Ashoka’s pillars carried there from Topra and Meerut; the historian Afif describes a cart of 42 wheels. No one can read them.
steps.today: Today: the Topra pillar stands on Firoz Shah Kotla, Delhi.

steps.title: Timur sacks Delhi
steps.text: After Firuz the sultanate weakens in succession quarrels. In 1398 Timur, the Central Asian conqueror, crosses the Indus. Before the battle at Delhi his memoirs say he had about 100,000 prisoners killed, a figure that is disputed. He defeats the sultan in December and Delhi is sacked for days. He leaves with captives, including stonemasons for Samarkand.
steps.today: Today: Timur’s Bibi Khanum mosque in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, used builders taken from India.

steps.title: Sultans of the regions
steps.text: Governors become kings: Jaunpur under the Sharqi sultans from 1394, Malwa from 1401 with Mandu as its capital, and Gujarat from 1407, where Ahmad Shah founds Ahmedabad in 1411. From 1414 the Sayyids rule a shrunken Delhi, at first as deputies of Timur’s son. Regional courts build mosques, tombs and palaces in their own styles.
steps.today: Today: Mandu, Madhya Pradesh, with Hoshang Shah’s marble tomb and the Jahaz Mahal.

steps.title: The Lodis and Jaunpur
steps.text: In 1451 Bahlol Lodi, an Afghan governor of the Punjab, takes Delhi. Later Afghan histories say he sat with his nobles on a carpet rather than a throne. He fights the Sharqi sultans of Jaunpur for about a quarter of a century and finally takes their kingdom in 1479. The Sharqis leave Jaunpur’s great Atala and Jama mosques.
steps.today: Today: Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Sikandar Lodi founds Agra
steps.text: Bahlol’s son Sikandar Lodi conquers Bihar and makes Agra his capital, building a new town there from about 1504. He writes Persian verse under the pen name Gulrukhi and orders a Persian book on medicine drawn from Sanskrit works. His yard measure (gaz) is used until Akbar’s time. The chronicles also record temples destroyed at Mathura.
steps.today: Today: Sikandar Lodi’s tomb stands in the Lodi Gardens, Delhi.

steps.title: Weavers and saints
steps.text: In the late sultanate, poet-saints sing in everyday speech. Kabir, a weaver of Varanasi, mocks empty ritual in Hindu and Muslim faith alike; his dates are uncertain, and tradition tells of a clash with Sikandar Lodi. Guru Nanak, who worked for a Lodi governor at Sultanpur, founds the Sikh faith and laments Babur’s invasion in his verses.
steps.today: Today: Kabir Chaura, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, and Gurdwara Ber Sahib, Sultanpur Lodhi, Punjab.

steps.title: The end at Panipat
steps.text: Ibrahim Lodi quarrels with his Afghan nobles, and Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of the Punjab, invites Babur from Kabul. At Panipat, Babur’s smaller army, with field guns and matchlocks, defeats Ibrahim’s much larger force; Babur’s own estimate of its size is disputed. Ibrahim dies on the field, and the Delhi Sultanate gives way to the Mughals.
steps.today: Today: Ibrahim Lodi’s tomb, Panipat, Haryana.

steps.title: The sultanate’s legacy
steps.text: For three centuries Delhi was a capital of the Islamic world. The sultans brought Persian government, the true arch and dome, and new towns and forts. From the mix of Persian and local speech grew Hindavi, an ancestor of Hindi and Urdu, and Amir Khusrau’s songs live on in qawwali. The Qutb Minar became a World Heritage site in 1993.
steps.today: Today: the Qutb complex, Tughlaqabad, Hauz Khas and the Lodi Gardens, Delhi.

items.name: Muhammad of Ghor
items.text: Muizzuddin Muhammad ruled Ghazni for his elder brother, the Ghurid sultan, and led the armies east. Beaten by the Chalukyas of Gujarat in 1178 and by Prithviraj in 1191, he came back each time. His victory at Tarain in 1192 opened north India. He left its rule to trusted slave commanders, and was killed in 1206.

items.name: Prithviraj Chauhan
items.text: Prithviraj III of the Chahamana (Chauhan) dynasty ruled from Ajmer. He beat Muhammad of Ghor in 1191 but lost to him the next year. Later poems, above all the Prithviraj Raso, made him a hero of romance, with his elopement with Samyukta of Kannauj and a legendary revenge in Ghazni. Historians treat these as tradition.

items.name: Muinuddin Chishti
items.text: Born in Sistan, Muinuddin Chishti brought the Chishti order of Sufis to India and settled at Ajmer. His teaching stressed love of God, music in worship and generosity to the poor. Pilgrims gather at his shrine each year for his death anniversary (urs). His successors, among them Nizamuddin Auliya, spread the order across India.

items.name: Qutbuddin Aibak
items.text: A Turkish slave bought as a boy, Aibak became Muhammad of Ghor’s commander in India. He took Delhi, began the Qutb Minar and its mosque, and after his master’s death in 1206 ruled independently from Lahore. Chroniclers praise his open-handedness. He died in 1210 when his horse fell during a game of polo (chaugan).

items.name: Bakhtiyar Khalji
items.text: Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji, a soldier of fortune, won lands in Awadh and raided Bihar. Minhaj says he took Nadia with only a small band of riders, and the Sena king fled. He ruled from Lakhnauti and set up mosques and colleges. His march toward Tibet ended in disaster, and he died soon after his return.

items.name: Minhaj-i Siraj
items.text: Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani fled the Mongols to Delhi and served the sultans as judge and preacher. His Tabaqat-i Nasiri, finished about 1260, is the main history of the Ghurids and the first Delhi sultans, including Bakhtiyar’s raids, Razia’s reign and the Mongol conquests, some of which he lived through.

items.name: Iltutmish
items.text: Shamsuddin Iltutmish, a Turk sold as a slave in his youth, was bought by Aibak, married his daughter and governed Badaun. As sultan he made Delhi the capital, won recognition from the caliph and kept clear of the Mongols. He chose his daughter Razia as his heir over his sons.

items.name: Razia Sultan
items.text: Razia was the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate. Minhaj, who served her, calls her wise, just and a fine general, and says she lacked only the fortune to have been born a man. She held court in public and led her armies herself. A revolt of nobles ended her reign within four years.

items.name: Ghiyasuddin Balban
items.text: One of Iltutmish’s slaves, Balban rose to rule first as minister and then as sultan. He made the court grand and severe, used spies and harsh punishments, crushed bandits around Delhi and a revolt in Bengal, and guarded the frontier. The death of his son in 1285 is said to have broken him.

items.name: Alauddin Khalji
items.text: Alauddin seized the throne by killing his uncle and made the sultanate a great power. He beat back the Mongols, controlled prices and taxed land heavily to pay his army, took Gujarat and the Rajput forts, and drew tribute from the far south. His last years were troubled, and his dynasty ended four years after him.

items.name: Malik Kafur
items.text: Taken at Khambhat in 1299, Kafur rose from slave to viceroy (malik naib). He led the campaigns to Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai, returning with enormous treasure. After Alauddin’s death he tried to rule through a child sultan, but was killed by palace guards within weeks.

items.name: Amir Khusrau
items.text: Amir Khusrau served sultans from Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq and wrote histories in verse of their wars. A disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, he wrote in Persian and in Hindavi, and called himself a ‘parrot of India’. Tradition credits him with the qawwali and with musical inventions that historians doubt. He is buried near his teacher.

items.name: Nizamuddin Auliya
items.text: Nizamuddin Auliya kept an open kitchen and hospice outside Delhi for rich and poor alike and stayed away from the court. His sayings, recorded by a disciple, were read for centuries. Several sultans distrusted him. He died in 1325, months after Ghiyasuddin, and his shrine in Delhi still draws crowds for its evening qawwali.

items.name: Ziauddin Barani
items.text: Barani was a courtier of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and finished his Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi under Firuz Shah. It is the main source for Alauddin’s markets and Muhammad’s experiments. He wrote with strong opinions about rank, religion and good kingship, so historians read him with care.

items.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
items.text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq was scholarly, generous and quick to punish. He ruled the largest area of any Delhi sultan, and tried bold schemes: a second capital in the Deccan, token coins and plans for distant conquests. Most failed, revolts spread, and he spent his last years on campaign. Historians still argue over him.

items.name: Ibn Battuta
items.text: Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 on pilgrimage and kept travelling for nearly thirty years, from West Africa to China. He spent about eight years in Delhi as a judge under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, whose court he describes in vivid detail. His Rihla, dictated after his return, is a key source for the sultanate.

items.name: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
items.text: Firuz Shah ruled for 37 years, building canals, towns, gardens and a hospital, and repairing older monuments, among them the Qutb Minar. He favoured the religious scholars, taxed Hindus more heavily and kept a huge household of slaves. In a short memoir he lists his good works. Weak successors followed him.

items.name: Timur
items.text: Timur, known in Europe as Tamerlane, built an empire from Anatolia to Central Asia from his capital, Samarkand. His Indian campaign of 1398 to 1399 was a raid for plunder, not a conquest, but it left Delhi ruined. His descendant Babur would return in 1526 and stay.

items.name: Bahlol Lodi
items.text: An Afghan of the Lodi clan, Bahlol rose as governor of Sirhind in the Punjab and took Delhi from the last Sayyid. He drew Afghan settlers into India and shared power with his nobles. His long war with Jaunpur restored much of the old sultanate’s heartland.

items.name: Sikandar Lodi
items.text: Sikandar Lodi, Bahlol’s son, was the strongest of the Lodis. He conquered Bihar, founded the new town of Agra and moved his court there. He patronised Persian learning and wrote poetry, and was strict in religious matters. His measures of land were used long after him.

items.name: Kabir
items.text: Kabir was a weaver (julaha) of Varanasi whose short sayings and songs reject caste and outward ritual and seek God within. They were passed on by singers and later written down in collections such as the Bijak and the Guru Granth Sahib. Hindus and Muslims both claimed him; tradition says both wished to bury or burn his body.

items.name: Guru Nanak
items.text: Born at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan, Nanak worked as a storekeeper for Daulat Khan Lodi at Sultanpur. Tradition says that about 1499, after vanishing into the river Bein for three days, he emerged saying there is no Hindu and no Muslim. He travelled widely and settled at Kartarpur, where a community grew around him.

items.name: Ibrahim Lodi
items.text: Ibrahim Lodi tried to rule his proud Afghan nobles more strictly than his father had, and many turned against him. Daulat Khan Lodi and Ibrahim’s uncle Alam Khan looked to Babur for help. Ibrahim died fighting at Panipat, the only Delhi sultan killed on the battlefield.
